newsitem.title: UK: BSkyB, OzEmail in Internet advertising venture.
newsitem.headline: BSkyB, OzEmail in Internet advertising venture.

text.p: British Sky Broadcasting, the satellite television company controlled by Rupert Murdoch, and an Australian Internet service company said on Wednesday they had formed a joint venture designed to harness the vast global advertising potential of the Internet.
BSkyB and Sydney-based OzEmail Ltd said they would invest equally in the joint venture, which was aimed at capitalising on the thousands of World Wide Web sites on the Internet.

The companies said the venture would be based on technology developed by OzEmail and would deliver advertising opportunities targeted at local audiences on Web sites throughout the world, regardless of where the Web site was hosted.

"From its inception BSkyB has been at the cutting edge of communications technology," BSkyB chief executive Sam Chisholm said in a statement. "We are delighted to be associated with OzEmail in this venture, which we regard as one of the world's most innovative and aggressive Internet companies."

OzEmail chairman Malcolum Turnbull said in a statement: "With global Internet advertising revenue expected to exceed $5 billion by the turn of the century, this new medium represents both a sizeable and an exciting opportunity,"

Turnbull and Elisabeth Murdoch, general manager of broadcasting for BSkyB, were named co-chairmen of the new joint venture. The two companies said details of the joint venture's technology and its strategy would be announced at the venture's launch on December 3 in New York.
Officials of the two companies were not available for comment.
But analysts and advertising executives involved in the Internet and new media opportunities said the venture was an attempt to bring order to a huge but chaotic marketplace.
"Internet advertising revenue is this great pot of gold out there," Deborah Monas, a multimedia analyst with Kagan World Media in England, told Reuters in a phone interview.
Advertising, she said, "is the only way out there to make money off the Internet. Unfortunately, it's not working yet."
Monas said she expected the joint venture would form a link between BSkyB's huge market in digital television and the Internet.

BSkyB, whose television interests stretch from Britain and across Europe to Asia, has previously said that it plans to offer access to the Internet via conventional television sets when it launches its digital service in Britain in 1997.
"I think the Internet is going to be a big part of digital television services," Monas said. "They're going to use that satellite beam as a way of getting onto the Internet."

One of the great frustrations for current users of the Internet is the slowness of the current telecommunications links, making it difficult to log onto Web sites at certain times of day and very time consuming to download some sites -- particularly those with elaborate graphics.
"Satellite gives you much more bandwidth than a telephone," said Monas. "You don't have to wait 10 minutes. You can have moving pictures and music."
